Adding another real-world data point to reinforce the urgency of this issue.

**Environment**: Windows 11, OpenCode latest, E:\opencode-data\
**Scale**: `opencode.db` grew to **36 GB** before disk exhaustion forced a full database recreation (lost all session history).

**Root cause confirmed**: the `part` table's `data` column accumulates full JSON-serialized tool outputs — every `bash`, `grep`, `read` invocation — and never releases them. With heavy use of `task()` (sub-agent delegation), child sessions proliferate and compound the problem. `auto_vacuum = OFF` means even if data were pruned, the file would never shrink.

**Impact**: E drive ran out of space at 36 GB, SQLite WAL write failed, OpenCode couldn't persist new events → entire database was recreated from scratch. All session history, compaction snapshots, and project state were lost.

This is not a theoretical concern — it's a data loss vector in production use. The fix is straightforward: `PRAGMA auto_vacuum = INCREMENTAL` set before table creation (or via a one-time migration). Would be happy to help test a PR.

Confirmed on OpenCode 1.17.6, WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04, Windows Terminal.
Captured via `script -q -c "opencode ." /tmp/oc.log` and analyzed hex dump.

Features ENABLED at startup but NOT disabled on exit via /exit:

| Feature | Enable seq | Disable seq on exit |
|---------|-----------|---------------------|
| Alt screen buffer | \033[?1049h | MISSING |
| Mouse basic | \033[?1000h | MISSING |
| Mouse button | \033[?1002h | MISSING |
| Mouse any | \033[?1003h | MISSING |
| SGR mouse | \033[?1006h | MISSING |
| Bracketed paste | \033[?2004h | MISSING |
| Focus reporting | \033[?1004h | OK (\033[?1004l) |

**Workaround**

Add this wrapper function to `~/.bashrc`:

```bash
oc() {
    opencode "$@"
    stty sane
    printf '\033[?1049l\033[?1000l\033[?1002l\033[?1003l\033[?1006l\033[?2004l\033[?1004l'
    reset
}
```

For reference on how other agents draw this line: **agent-manual** (https://github.com/Ar9av/agent-manual) cross-documents slash commands vs. hooks across 17 agents.

The clearest separation is Claude Code's model: slash commands (`.claude/commands/<name>.md`) are agent-facing — they inject a prompt into the conversation. Hooks (`settings.json` under `hooks`) are programmatic — they fire on lifecycle events and can block, transform, or observe without the agent knowing. The two systems never overlap.

Gemini CLI follows the same split: Agent Skills (on-demand Markdown procedures) vs. Hooks (event-driven scripts). Codex doesn't have a slash command system yet, so hooks handle both roles.

If OpenCode goes the same route, the key design question from the almanac data is whether slash commands can trigger hooks or vice versa — Claude Code keeps them strictly separate, which makes both simpler to reason about individually.

@jphein @klietus really appreciate your comments! 

Tbh, I've recently moved away from using OpenCode as my daily driver and now primarily use AdaL CLI from Sylph AI. This change actually led me to build a tool called adal-compress, which is a local HTTP proxy that compresses token payloads at the wire level before they reach the model. I've made it available on GitHub at https://github.com/chindris-mihai-alexandru/adal-cli/tree/main/adal-compress.

One of the benefits of this approach is that it doesn't require any specific invocation discipline, it just applies deterministic rule-based compression to every request. I have to say that I kept running into the issue of the substrate beating the orchestrator, but by using rule-based compression at the proxy layer, I've been able to sidestep this problem entirely, and in practice, I've seen savings of 50-93% on exploration-heavy sessions.

The work being done on building a queryable memory that the model navigates is a different and harder problem than what I've been working on. While I'm focusing on compressing the data that gets sent, this other approach is building a complex system with multiple components, and I'll def have a look over the SignalZero-Desktop codebase to learn more about it.

> > Its like people never dealt with contracts and suppliers?
> > OpenCode negotiates with DeepSeek for a discount based upon the original API Prices. They get a discount, that is their profit margin. This is a contract between OpenCode and DeepSeek.
> > When DeepSeek reduces the prices for their own platform by 75%, this has nothing to do with the established contract. OpenCode may not be happy about this, but they are buying a service from DeepSeek, on DeepSeek's terms.
> > OpenCode can go back to DeepSeek and try to renegotiate the contract but the ball is in DeepSeek court, they have the power as the supplier of the good.
> > I am 100% sure that OpenCode has already tried to get a better contract. That is typical business practice on sudden changes.
> > > I was wondering why is Zen also priced at 4x?
> > 
> > 
> > See above. And because OpenCode is a legal company that need to make money in a legit way.
> > Can they be sneakily try to connect to DeepSeek their API service and use those cheaper API directly from DeepSeek. Sure, and they can then get banned from the platform, and have their contract annulled (if found out).
> > This is not how legal companies work. And your still forgetting that OpenCode makes no money on this backdoor approach. They will lose money with needing tons of IPs and other tricks to bypass any detection mechanics on DeepSeeks side. So any price will always be higher then what DeepSeek offers.
> > Legit companies do not try to pull that stuff because it opens them up to a ton of legal issues. Not just with DeepSeek but with any other API provider, as they will not do business with you (if caught doing gray stuff).
> > So, as long as DeepSeek does not offer a better contractual term, OpenCode is stuck on the old contract.
> > Right now, DeepSeek is focused on gaining market share themselves. Even if that is at the cost of business clients. Yea, it sucks but this happens a lot in the industry where are is a high demand for a product, and the supplier of that product decided to "cut out" the middle man. As in, becomes a competitor to its own clients.

Imagine this use-case:
You have a very well-defined set of prompts for different agents and an overall configuration that you want to follow you on any machine (think work/personal). Instead of having a "traditional" remote development setup where the project repos live on the remote server, you could just use the opencode server, its configuration and tools etc. but configure the session's cwd to be a client-local directory on any client spawned from any machine.

This workflow could use the ssh patching through rsync feature in the background and hide it in a flag as so:
`opencode attach --local-dir /path/to/local/project`

What this PR does: This PR enables plan mode by default in the CLI. Previously, plan mode was gated behind the experimentalPlanMode feature flag, requiring users to set OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL=1 or OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_PLAN_MODE=1 environment variables to use it. With this change, the plan agent, plan_exit tool, and the yes/no confirmation flow for switching from plan to build agent are always available without any configuration. Changes made (3 files): 1. runtime-flags.ts: Changed experimentalPlanMode from enabledByExperimental(...) to Config.succeed(true) — always enabled. 2. reminders.ts: Removed the legacy non-experimental code path and unused imports (PROMPT_PLAN, MessageV2). 3. registry.ts: Removed the flags.experimentalPlanMode guard from plan tool registration — now loads whenever flags.client === "cli". Verification: - Ran bun run _verify-plan-mode.ts — confirmed experimentalPlanMode: true - Ran bun run --cwd packages/opencode --conditions=browser src/index.ts — TUI starts successfully with plan mode active - Plan agent appears in agent selector, plan_exit tool is registered
